title: Every Plant-Based Food Tested Had a Fungal Toxin — but Don't Panic
summary:
Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods and drinks — and every single one contained at least one fungal toxin. The products included vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond and soy milk sold in the UK.

The toxins are called mycotoxins. They are poisonous substances made by certain fungi, including molds, and they can get into food when crops are contaminated while growing, being harvested or stored. Researchers found at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many products contained several.

Before you panic, here is the reassuring part. Every product contained mycotoxin levels below the European Union's recommended guideline levels. The researchers, led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy with help from Cranfield University, said that reflected the high food quality standards of the UK food industry.

Mycotoxins are chemicals, not living mold, so finding one does not automatically mean a food is unsafe. The risk depends on the type of toxin, how much is present and how much a person eats over time. Eating one of these products now and then is unlikely to cause problems at the levels found.

The bigger question is repeated exposure. Earlier studies suggest that small amounts eaten regularly may add up over time. At high enough levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys and interfere with the immune system — but the new findings do not show that the tested products cause these problems.

"Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided," said Andrea Patriarca, a senior lecturer in mycology at Cranfield University. "As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products."
why_it_matters: Plant-based foods are popular, so knowing what is in them — and that the levels found were safe — helps families make calm, informed choices.

background_read: Fungi are living things that include mushrooms and molds, and some of them make poisonous substances called mycotoxins.
These toxins can get into crops while they are growing, being harvested or stored, and from there into the foods made from those crops.
Food safety experts set guideline levels — the highest amounts they consider safe — and food is tested to check it stays below those levels.
The risk from a toxin usually depends on how much of it there is and how often a person eats it over time.
